opts: What the drug does to the body
What the body does to the drug
How the drug interacts with receptors
The side effect profile of the drug
questions.exp: Pharmacokinetics = absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion (ADME) — body's effects on drug.

opts: How the body eliminates the drug
The effect of the drug on the body
The rate of drug excretion only
The formulation type of the drug
The manufacturing process of the drug
questions.exp: Pharmacodynamics = drug effects on receptors and tissues (mechanism of action, dose-response).

questions.q: Which receptor type produces the FASTEST response?
questions.exp: Ligand-gated ion channels (e.g. nicotinic ACh) open in milliseconds — the fastest response.
β-adrenergic receptors are GPCRs (Gs → cAMP). Insulin = RTK, nicotinic = LGIC, cortisol = nuclear, NMDA = LGIC.

questions.q: Which is an example of a ligand-gated ion channel?
questions.exp: Nicotinic ACh receptors are pentameric LGICs that flux Na⁺/K⁺ when ACh binds.

questions.q: Insulin receptor is an example of a(n):
questions.exp: Insulin binds an RTK, triggering autophosphorylation, IRS, and downstream PI3K/MAPK signalling.
Steroid and thyroid hormones are lipid-soluble; they enter the cell and bind intracellular/nuclear receptors to alter gene expression.

questions.q: A full agonist is a drug that:
opts: It has no effect on the receptor
It produces a maximal response at the receptor
It produces a partial response at the receptor
questions.exp: Full agonists fully activate the receptor (efficacy = 1). Partial agonists give submaximal response even at full occupancy.
optExp: That would be no binding/no efficacy.

opts: It cannot be overcome by increasing agonist concentration
It can be overcome by increasing the concentration of agonist
It has an efficacy of one
It is the same as a partial agonist
questions.exp: Competitive antagonists shift the dose-response curve rightward; full Emax can still be reached with enough agonist.
optExp: Partial agonists have some intrinsic activity.

questions.q: The main site of oral drug absorption is the:
questions.exp: The small intestine, with villi and microvilli, has the largest absorptive surface area for oral drugs.
optExp: Stomach absorbs some acidic drugs but smaller area.
Colon absorbs water and some drugs.
Mouth allows sublingual absorption for some.

opts: Metabolism of the drug in the intestines only
Metabolism and inactivation of the drug by the liver before systemic circulation
The binding of the drug to plasma proteins
The absorption of the drug through the skin
questions.exp: Drugs absorbed from the gut pass through the liver via portal circulation, where significant metabolism can occur before reaching systemic circulation.
optExp: Intestinal first-pass is a component but liver dominates.

questions.exp: IV, sublingual, and (partially) rectal routes bypass the liver's portal circulation.
optExp: SC enters systemic but is not the most common bypass route mentioned.

opts: Conjugation reactions with glutathione or other molecules
Binding of the drug to plasma proteins
questions.exp: Phase I involves functional group modifications by CYP450 (oxidation), reductases, and hydrolases.
Phase II adds polar groups (glucuronide, sulfate, glutathione) to make drugs water-soluble for excretion.

questions.q: A drug with a high volume of distribution (Vd) implies:
opts: The drug is restricted to plasma
The drug distributes extensively into tissues
The drug is excreted unchanged in urine
The drug cannot cross cell membranes
The drug has poor oral absorption
questions.exp: High Vd suggests the drug leaves plasma and distributes extensively into tissues (e.g. lipophilic drugs, tissue-binding drugs).
optExp: High Vd actually means easy crossing.
Vd is about distribution, not absorption.

questions.q: The major route of drug excretion is:
questions.exp: Most drugs are excreted by the kidneys via filtration, secretion, and limited reabsorption.
optExp: Some drugs excreted in sweat but minor.

questions.q: A weakly acidic drug is best excreted in:
questions.exp: Weak acids are more ionised in alkaline urine → less reabsorbed → faster excretion. This is the basis of urinary alkalinisation in aspirin overdose.
optExp: Acidic urine keeps weak acids non-ionised, increasing reabsorption.
Dehydration concentrates urine but doesn't enhance excretion.

opts: The fraction of drug reaching systemic circulation
The ability to bind to receptors
questions.exp: Bioavailability = (AUC oral / AUC IV) × 100%. IV drugs have F = 100%.
optExp: Concentration is a measurement, not definition.
Therapeutic index is a safety metric.

questions.q: Half-life (t½) is the time for plasma drug concentration to:
opts: The time to reach steady state
The time for plasma concentration to decrease by 50%
The time for complete drug elimination
The time for plasma protein binding to occur
The time to reach maximum concentration (Cmax)
questions.exp: t½ = time for plasma concentration to fall to half its value. After 4-5 half-lives, ~94-97% of drug is eliminated.
optExp: Steady state takes ~4-5 t½ with regular dosing.
Protein binding is a separate property.

opts: An ionised form of the drug
Poor blood flow at the absorption site
questions.exp: Lipid-soluble drugs cross membranes more easily → better absorption.

questions.q: CYP450 enzymes are mainly found in the:
questions.exp: CYP450 enzymes are most concentrated in hepatocyte smooth ER, performing most of Phase I drug metabolism.
optExp: Brain has some CYPs but minor.

opts: The free active concentration of drug
questions.exp: Only free (unbound) drug can leave the plasma to act on receptors or be metabolised/excreted. Highly bound drugs have prolonged effects.
optExp: Binding affects distribution/elimination more than absorption.
Affects more than just Phase I.

questions.q: The therapeutic index (TI) is defined as:
opts: Calculated as ED50 divided by LD50
Calculated as LD50 divided by ED50
Calculated as Cmax divided by Cmin
Calculated as Vd divided by Cl
Calculated as dose multiplied by half-life
questions.exp: TI = LD50/ED50 (lethal dose for 50% / effective dose for 50%). Higher = safer drug (wider window).

opts: The maximum effect a drug can produce
The dose required to produce a given effect
The volume of distribution of the drug
questions.exp: Potency relates to position on the dose-response curve (EC50). High potency = effect at low dose. Efficacy = max effect.

opts: The dose needed for therapeutic effect
The maximum response the drug can produce
The time to onset of action
questions.exp: Efficacy = the maximum effect (Emax). Full agonists have high efficacy; partial agonists have lower efficacy.

opts: Produces no effect on the receptor
Reduces constitutive activity below basal levels
Has an efficacy value of one
questions.exp: Inverse agonists stabilise the inactive receptor conformation, reducing constitutive activity below baseline.
optExp: That is a neutral antagonist (in some descriptions).
Different mechanism — antagonist has zero efficacy, not negative.

opts: Rapid development of tolerance despite continued use
questions.exp: Tachyphylaxis = acute desensitisation over minutes-hours with repeated administration.

opts: Inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis
questions.exp: Penicillins (β-lactams) inhibit penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) needed for cross-linking peptidoglycan.
Aminoglycosides bind the 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA and inhibiting protein synthesis.
Macrolides bind the 50S subunit, blocking peptide chain elongation.
Quinolones inhibit DNA gyrase (gram-negative) and topoisomerase IV (gram-positive), preventing DNA replication.
Sulfonamides inhibit dihydropteroate synthase; trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase — both block folate-dependent nucleotide synthesis.

questions.q: Tachyphylaxis differs from tolerance in that tachyphylaxis develops:
opts: Over weeks to months with continuous drug exposure
Over minutes to hours with repeated dosing
Only in elderly patients receiving treatment
Only with placebo and inactive compounds
questions.exp: Tachyphylaxis = rapid (acute) desensitisation. Tolerance develops over days-weeks.

opts: Clearance rate depends on drug concentration
Constant amount of drug eliminated per unit time
Half-life remains constant at all drug concentrations
Drug is eliminated instantly without metabolic delay
questions.exp: Zero-order: elimination rate is constant (e.g. ethanol). At any concentration above saturation, a fixed amount is removed per unit time.
optExp: Half-life varies with concentration in zero-order.

opts: Constant amount of drug eliminated per unit time
Constant fraction of drug eliminated per unit time
No elimination of drug occurs during therapy
Enzyme is saturated at all drug concentrations
Drug elimination follows a linear dose-response relationship
questions.exp: First-order: rate of elimination is proportional to concentration; a constant FRACTION is removed per t (most drugs).

opts: Binds reversibly to the orthosteric receptor site
Cannot be overcome by increasing agonist concentration
Produces a rightward shift in the dose-response curve
Increases the affinity of agonist for receptor
Binds to an allosteric site distinct from the agonist binding site
questions.exp: Non-competitive (or irreversible) antagonists prevent the agonist from achieving full Emax even at high concentrations.

opts: Prevents peptidoglycan synthesis in the bacterial cell wall
Disrupts the bacterial cell membrane integrity
questions.exp: Vancomycin blocks Gram-positive cell wall synthesis by binding D-Ala-D-Ala — used for MRSA, C. difficile.

questions.q: A patient with cirrhosis is at increased risk of toxicity from drugs metabolised by:
questions.exp: Cirrhotic livers have reduced CYP450 capacity, so drugs metabolised by Phase I hepatic pathways accumulate.
optExp: Renal-cleared drugs are less affected by liver disease.

questions.exp: Naloxone competitively antagonises μ-opioid receptors, reversing opioid respiratory depression in overdose.
Atropine competitively blocks muscarinic ACh receptors → ↑ HR, dry mouth, dilated pupils, bronchodilation.
Tetracyclines bind 30S ribosomal subunit, blocking aminoacyl-tRNA entry to the A site — bacteriostatic.

questions.q: Steady state plasma concentration is achieved after approximately:
questions.exp: With regular dosing, steady state (input rate = output rate) is reached after ~4-5 half-lives (about 94-97% of steady state).
